spec.title: Peel the image, read the control baked in
spec.intro:
An image is the unit a control claim is made about — "containers don't run as root," "no secrets
in the image," "only the service port is exposed." You are handed two REAL OCI images: a clean
stock alpine and a misconfigured twin built by a real `docker build`, and asked to read each claim
straight off the image's manifest and config, find the secret baked into a layer, and click the
exact field where the twin contradicts its claim.

This surface is the image, rendered as nested selectable regions: the config (User, ExposedPorts,
Env, Cmd) and the manifest's ordered layer descriptors, each with its real sha256 digest. Every
value you reveal is the OCI reader's real decode of the real blob — the same field `docker inspect`
shows, and the layer's secret is read straight from the real (decompressed) tar by the same pattern
set a secret scanner uses. Nothing is invented; the image is the answer key. Start on the broken
twin.

items.label: Virtual machine (hardware-virtualized guest)
items.keyRef: NIST 800-190 §2.1 (VM = own guest kernel; container = shared host kernel)

items.label: Container (namespace/cgroup isolation)
items.keyRef: NIST 800-190 §2.1 / §2.3 (containers share the host kernel — a larger blast radius)

tasks.instruction:
On the misconfigured twin, descend into the `image config` and select the `User` field. Read
the uid the container runs as. This field decides the "containers don't run as root" claim (CM-6).

hints.nudge: The runtime config says who the process runs as — find the User field inside the config region.

hints.concept: §4.2 — OCI config.User is the effective uid; uid 0 = root (CIS Docker 4.1 / CM-6)

hints.reveal: Select config → User; it reads root → ROOT (uid 0), the CM-6 finding

tasks.explain:
`User: root` makes every process in the container uid 0 — a CIS Docker 4.1 / CM-6 finding. The
reader read it straight off the real config the build produced; the hardened ideal is an explicit
non-root uid. (Note the honest subtlety: stock alpine has no `User` at all, which per the OCI
runtime default ALSO means root — the twin just makes the dangerous default explicit.)

tasks.instruction:
Still on the misconfigured twin, select the config's `ExposedPorts` field. Read which ports the
image declares it listens on. This field decides the "only the service port is exposed" claim (CM-7).

hints.nudge: The config lists every port the image advertises — find ExposedPorts.

hints.concept: §4.2 — ExposedPorts is the declared listening surface; an extra port is a CM-7 finding

hints.reveal: Select config → ExposedPorts; it reads 22/tcp, 8080/tcp — SSH exposed alongside the app port

tasks.explain:
The build `EXPOSE`d 22 (SSH) alongside the 8080 app port. Least functionality (CM-7 / CIS Docker
5.7) says expose only what the service needs; an SSH port on an app image is the finding. The
number came off the real config, not your guess.

tasks.instruction:
Open the `image manifest` and select the topmost layer descriptor (`layer1`). Read how many
layers this image has and the topmost layer's real sha256 digest — the provenance you cite.

hints.nudge: An image is an ordered stack of content-addressed layers — the manifest lists them as descriptors.

hints.concept: §4.3 — manifest.layers[] is ordered; each descriptor is a sha256 digest you cite as provenance

hints.reveal: Select layer 1 (the topmost descriptor); its digest is sha256:48092d72… (178 bytes)

tasks.explain:
The misconfigured twin has two layers; the topmost (`layer1`, sha256:48092d72…, 178 bytes) is the
one the build ADDED on top of the stock rootfs. A layer's digest is content-addressed — it is the
provenance you cite when you find something in it, which is exactly the next task.

tasks.instruction:
Peel layer 1's tar and select the baked-secret region (`layer1.secret`). Report the secret's
filename and the layer digest that carries it. This is the "no secrets in the image" claim (IA-5).

hints.nudge: A secret added in one layer survives even if a later layer "removes" it — peel the layer that added it.

hints.concept: §4.4 — each layer is a content-addressed tar diff; the secret lives in the layer that ADDED it

hints.reveal: Select layer1.secret — the reader's tar walk found /app-credentials.env, cited by sha256:48092d72…

tasks.explain:
The reader decompressed the real layer tar, and the secret-scanner pattern set tripped on a real
AWS-style credential in `/app-credentials.env`. The secret glows in the layer that added it, cited
by its digest — IA-5 / SC-28 / CIS Docker 4.10. A `RUN rm` in a later layer would not erase it.

tasks.instruction:
Move to the findings board. Map each of the three findings (runs-as-root, exposed ports, baked
secret) onto its CIS/NIST control zone, then place the VM and container cards onto the kernel
each uses — to show which isolates more strongly and why.

hints.nudge: Each misconfiguration maps to a hardening control; isolation strength depends on whether you share a kernel.

hints.concept: §4.5 — runs-as-root→CM-6, extra port→CM-7, baked secret→IA-5/SC-28; VM=own kernel, container=shared kernel

hints.reveal: runs-as-root→CM-6; exposed ports→CM-7; baked secret→IA-5/SC-28; VM→own host kernel; container→shared host kernel

tasks.explain:
The findings the reader surfaced now carry framework refs (CIS Docker + NIST 800-190 + 800-53),
and the VM-vs-container split is the why: a VM runs its own guest kernel, a container shares the
host's — so a container escape has a larger blast radius. The mapping is the cited key, the
findings are the real config.

tasks.instruction:
You already read the twin's `ExposedPorts` (22/tcp, 8080/tcp) in t2 — that is the broken half of
the finding. Now switch to the CLEAN panel and select its `ExposedPorts` to read the hardened
baseline the twin violates. The diff is real only once you have BOTH values: the same field, the
clean baseline AND the twin's value, the control, and the framework ref are your evidence finding.

hints.nudge: Both images are real and nearly identical — read the SAME field on the clean panel to get the baseline the twin diverges from.

hints.concept: §4.6 — a control is a predicate over the config; the diff is clean-baseline vs twin at ExposedPorts (CM-7)

hints.reveal: Switch to the clean panel, select config → ExposedPorts — it reads none, the baseline the twin's 22/tcp, 8080/tcp violates

tasks.explain:
The discriminating field is the reader's computed divergence over two real images, not your
opinion: the clean image exposes nothing (none), the twin exposes 22 + 8080 — CM-7 / CIS Docker
5.7. Reading BOTH halves is what makes it a diff, not a single observation: your finding names the
field (ExposedPorts), both values (none vs 22/tcp, 8080/tcp), the control (CM-7), and the ref — and
anyone can re-derive it by `docker save`-ing the same tags.

tasks.instruction:
In 4–6 sentences, for a non-technical colleague: explain the difference between a VM (its own
guest kernel, hardware-virtualized) and a container (shares the host kernel, isolated by
namespaces and cgroups), and why that difference changes the blast radius of a compromise. Then
explain why a secret baked into an image layer survives even after a later layer "deletes" the
file. Use the §3 shipping-container model, not jargon.

hints.nudge: The §3 model: a VM ships its own engine room; containers share the ship's engine but get their own locked cabin.
